bug_description.normalized: The staged 69-byte witness is a single `.include ` directive followed by a 60-byte pathname operand. In `crypto/conf/conf_def.c`, `def_load_bio()` copies that operand into `include`, and `process_include()` immediately calls `stat(include, &st)`; the path does not resolve in the saved run, so the error-reporting branch executes. `FUNCerr("stat", errno)` reaches `ERR_add_error_data(2, "calling function ", func)`, whose first vulnerable `ERR_add_error_vdata()` call allocates an 81-byte heap buffer, fills it with `calling function stat`, and stores that pointer plus `err_data_size = 81` in the current error slot. `process_include()` then calls `ERR_add_error_data(1, include)` to append the attacker-controlled 60-byte pathname into the same buffer. On this second append, the reused buffer already holds 21 characters, so the combined string reaches exactly 81 characters before the terminator. The vulnerable code keeps the 81-byte allocation and still calls `OPENSSL_strlcat(str, arg, size + 1)`, so `OPENSSL_strlcpy()` writes the trailing NUL one byte past the heap object. The staged patch changes `FUNCerr` to `ERR_raise_data(..., "calling function %s", ...)`, removing this witness's first-call allocation/store and second-call reuse sequence through `ERR_put_func_error -> ERR_add_error_data`.

source.description: First project-code materialization of the attacker-controlled `.include` operand into the standalone pathname string later passed to `stat()` and appended into the error buffer.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` is exactly 69 bytes. Bytes 0..8 are ASCII `.include `, and bytes 9..68 are copied by `str_copy()` into `include` as a 60-byte pathname operand containing 56 `0xFF` bytes and 4 literal spaces, with no newline or embedded NUL.

root_cause.description: The reused error buffer is grown only when the append total is strictly greater than `size`, so the second append keeps the original 81-byte allocation even when the saved witness reaches the exact boundary `21 + 60 == 81` and still needs one more byte for the terminator.
root_cause.note: ASan shows the overflowed object was the 81-byte buffer allocated at line 865 during the first prefix append. On the second append, that buffer already contains the 21-character prefix `calling function stat` and the attacker-controlled `include` adds 60 more characters. Equality at `len == size == 81` therefore still leaves no room for the trailing NUL, but `if (len > size)` does not grow the buffer before `OPENSSL_strlcat(str, arg, size + 1)` uses it as though 82 bytes were available.

sink.description: Final out-of-bounds write in the saved ASan trace. `OPENSSL_strlcpy()` writes the terminating NUL one byte past the reused 81-byte error buffer.
sink.note: After `OPENSSL_strlcat()` skips over the 21-byte prefix, `OPENSSL_strlcpy()` receives `size == 61` for the 60-byte `include` string. It copies 60 attacker-controlled bytes into `str[21..80]` and then stores `\0` at `str[81]`, matching ASan's `WRITE of size 1` at `0x608000000171`, exactly one byte past the allocation `[0x608000000120,0x608000000171)`.

tainted_value_origin.description: The vulnerability-relevant tainted value is the 60-byte include pathname copied from the witness `.include` line. That exact string is later passed to `stat()` and then appended into the reused error buffer.

parser_admitted.description: The config parser recognizes the attacker-controlled key as `.include` and enters include-file handling instead of the ordinary `name=value` path.

coarse_trace.summary: The `.include` directive's operand is copied into the standalone `include` pathname string.
A failing `stat(include)` takes the error-reporting branch that first emits `calling function stat` and then appends the same pathname.
The first error-data append allocates an 81-byte heap buffer, fills it with `calling function stat`, and stores that pointer and size in the current error slot.
The second append reuses that stored 81-byte buffer, hits the exact `21 + 60 == 81` boundary, and does not grow the allocation before copying.
The helper writes the final terminator one byte past the 81-byte heap allocation.

fine_trace.note: Inside the `.include` branch, `str_copy()` copies the directive operand into a fresh pathname string. For the staged witness there are no quotes, escapes, or `$` expansions, so `include` is the raw 60-byte suffix of the PoC line.

The attacker-controlled pathname is used as the `stat()` target. In the saved Stage 01 run it does not resolve, so the branch executes `FUNCerr("stat", errno)` and then issues a second `ERR_add_error_data(1, include)` call that will append the same pathname string into the error text.

The first `ERR_add_error_data(2, "calling function ", func)` call finds no reusable error-data buffer, so it allocates a fresh 81-byte heap object and initializes it as an empty string. This is the exact allocation ASan later reports as the overflowed object.

After that same first call concatenates `calling function ` with `func == "stat"`, this helper stores the resulting `calling function stat` heap pointer in `es->err_data[i]` and records `es->err_data_size[i] = 81`. The stored string length is 21 characters, but the recorded capacity remains the original 81-byte allocation.

The second `ERR_add_error_data(1, include)` call takes the reuse branch. It reloads the previously stored heap pointer into `str` and the stored byte count `81` into `size`, so this append starts with an 81-byte object that already contains the 21-character prefix `calling function stat`.

At the second append, the reused buffer already contributes 21 characters and the attacker-controlled `include` contributes 60 more, so the concatenated string reaches exactly 81 characters. The growth check is still `if (len > size)`, so the equality case keeps the original 81-byte allocation even though 82 bytes are needed including the terminator. The saved witness therefore overflows at the exact boundary `21 + 60 == size == 81`.

Because step 6 did not reallocate, `OPENSSL_strlcat()` is called on the original 81-byte heap object with `(size_t)size + 1 == 82`. The destination already holds 21 bytes, so `OPENSSL_strlcat()` advances to `str + 21` and invokes `OPENSSL_strlcpy()` with remaining size 61 to copy the 60-byte attacker pathname.

With `size == 61` and a 60-byte source string, `OPENSSL_strlcpy()` copies 60 bytes into `str[21..80]` and then stores the terminator at `str[81]`. That is exactly one byte past the 81-byte allocation reported by ASan.

sanitizer_ground_truth.patch_resolves_note: The staged patch changes `FUNCerr(f,r)` from `ERR_PUT_func_error(ERR_LIB_SYS,(f),(r),...)` to `ERR_raise_data(ERR_LIB_SYS,(r),"calling function %s",(f))`. On this path `process_include()` therefore no longer reaches the vulnerable first `ERR_add_error_data(2, "calling function ", func)` call that allocates and stores the reusable 81-byte `err_data` buffer before the later attacker-controlled `include` append.

cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: ASan identifies the overflowed object as the 81-byte buffer allocated at `ERR_add_error_vdata` line 865 during the first prefix append. The rebuilt trace closes that allocation to the second append: the same pointer and `err_data_size = 81` are stored in `err_set_error_data_int()`, reloaded at lines 852-855, and then overrun when the 21-byte prefix plus the 60-byte `include` string hit the exact `len == size == 81` boundary before the terminator.

poc.trigger: Stage 01 saved `PYTHONPATH=gt_generation python3 -m gt_toolkit arvo-workspace --result-dir /mnt/datastore/gt_generation/gt_results/arvo_16107 run --version vulnerable --expect crash`, which fed the staged `poc` to `/out/conf` and reproduced `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE 1` in `OPENSSL_strlcpy` with stack `OPENSSL_strlcat -> ERR_add_error_vdata -> process_include`.

format.name: single `.include` directive with the saved 60-byte missing-path operand
format.contract: Exactly the 69-byte witness stored in `poc` (sha256 `e6251a14a1a1768d6c93ca8350dcdcd4ab434f85a58d8237054ad48e60b65d6a`). Bytes 0..8 are ASCII `.include ` and bytes 9..68 are the 60-byte include operand with no newline or embedded NUL; that operand contains 56 `0xFF` bytes and 4 literal spaces. In the saved run `str_copy()` materializes those 60 bytes into `include`, `stat(include)` fails, the earlier `calling function stat` prefix occupies 21 characters in the reused error buffer, and the second append therefore reaches exactly 81 characters before its terminating NUL. That witness-specific `21 + 60 == 81` boundary is what makes the vulnerable build write the terminator one byte past the 81-byte allocation.
